lesson.menu_title: If We Had Shipped by Friday -- Conditional Mastery
lesson.menu_desc: A late container and a better deal: mixed conditionals (if we had shipped..., we would have... now / if we weren't partners, we would have cancelled...) plus the words of a delay -- hindsight, knock-on effect, shortfall, surcharge, rush order, backorder, penalty, bargaining chip, deal-breaker, goodwill

lesson.grammar_point: mixed conditionals (if + past perfect, would + base verb / if + past simple, would have + past participle)

reading.rtitle: When a Shipment Is Late: Negotiate, Don't Blame
paras: Every company that ships goods will one day receive the call: the container missed the cut-off. The first reaction is usually to look back and find someone to blame. In hindsight, everything looks obvious. But that call is also the start of a negotiation, and what you say in the first ten minutes matters more than who made the mistake.

Start with the facts of today, not the story of last week. What is the shortfall, and what is the knock-on effect on your own customers? A good manager connects the past to the present in one sentence: "If the parts had arrived on Monday, our line would be running now." That sentence is not an accusation. It tells the supplier exactly what the delay costs.

Then look at the contract. If there is a penalty clause, it is a bargaining chip, not a weapon. Many buyers would rather receive a rush order with no surcharge than a small check six months later. And if you are a long-term customer, say so: "If we weren't partners, we would have cancelled the order already." The supplier hears two things at once: you are unhappy, and you want to stay.

Finally, protect the goodwill. One late container is rarely a deal-breaker; a second one, handled badly, often is. Write down what was agreed, including which items stay on backorder and when they will ship. The best calls after a delay end with both sides asking the same question: what would we do differently if this happened again?

listenings.text: I run operations at the joint venture in Houston, and last Friday was the worst day of my quarter. The container from Pittsburgh missed the cut-off by four hours. Four hours. If it had left on Friday, our customers would have their valves today, and I would not be on the phone every morning apologizing. Instead, we have a shortfall of two hundred units, and the knock-on effect is everywhere. One customer has already stopped his own production line. In hindsight, we made a mistake too. We did not keep any buffer stock in the warehouse. If we had kept even fifty units, we would be in a much better position now. So this week I am asking the supplier for a rush order, and I am not paying a surcharge for it.

When the supplier called me about the delay, my first idea was to cancel the whole contract. I did not do it, and I am glad. If I were a younger manager, I would have made that call in anger. Instead, I looked at what we had. The penalty clause gave us a bargaining chip, and we used it carefully. We told them that if we were not long-term partners, we would have cancelled already. Then we asked for something useful. They agreed to a rush order with no surcharge, and the two items on backorder will ship by air at their cost. In the end, we did not use the penalty at all. Goodwill is cheap to keep and very expensive to rebuild. The only deal-breaker for me now would be a second delay without a phone call.

extra_audio.text: First, you check the size of the shortfall and the knock-on effect on your customers. Then, you read the contract to see if there is a penalty clause. After that, you call the supplier and explain what the delay costs you today. Next, you ask for a rush order without a surcharge. Finally, you write down what was agreed, including the items on backorder.
